name: New York
tagline: Ambition, art and appetite, all at once, all night.
bestMonths: May, Jun, Jul, Aug and Sep
whenBlurb: Come late spring (May–June) or early autumn (Sept–Oct) for the city at its finest; skip the humid deep summer and the January freeze.

ourTake.lede: New York is a city of neighbourhoods, not landmarks; pick a base with a good coffee and a good bar and let the blocks around it be the trip. Book the restaurant of the moment weeks ahead and see one great museum properly rather than three in a blur, the Met alone is a full, unhurried day. Skip Times Square beyond a single glance and give the time instead to the West Village, the High Line at dawn, and the outer-borough tables the guidebooks miss.
ourTake.comeIf: You want the full weight of a great world city, galleries, tables, theatre, and shopping in a single week.
ourTake.skipIf: You are after quiet, nature, or a slow pace; this city never fully exhales.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Aman New York
items.description: A hushed vertical sanctuary in the Crown Building, the city, finally, on silent.

items.name: The Mark Hotel
credentials: World's 50 Best Hotels 2025 (No. 43, only NYC entry)
items.description: The Upper East Side's most glamorous house, the only New York hotel on the world list.

items.name: The Carlyle, A Rosewood Hotel
items.description: Old-New-York grandeur with a cabaret in the basement, the city's most storied address.

items.name: Casa Cipriani New York
items.description: A members'-club hotel in a landmark ferry terminal, Italian glamour on the water's edge.

items.name: The Greenwich Hotel, Tribeca Penthouse
items.description: A one-of-a-kind Japanese-crafted penthouse above the Greenwich, the city's most private suite.

items.name: The Peninsula New York
items.description: A Beaux-Arts landmark on Fifth, with the group's famous precision and a rooftop bar.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental, New York
items.description: Park-and-skyline views from on high at Columbus Circle, the group's calm, precise flagship.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel New York Downtown
items.description: The surest hands in Lower Manhattan, service you never have to think about.

items.name: The St. Regis New York
items.description: The house that invented the butler, Astor-era Beaux-Arts splendour off Fifth Avenue.

items.name: The Ritz-Carlton New York, Central Park
items.description: Park-facing tradition on Central Park South, grand, gracious, and reliably excellent.

items.name: Baccarat Hotel New York
items.description: Crystal-chandelier glamour opposite MoMA, a jewel-box of a hotel, and it knows it.

items.name: Park Hyatt New York
items.description: A calm, contemporary tower on Billionaires' Row, quiet luxury, beautifully run.

items.name: The Towers at Lotte New York Palace
items.description: A hotel-within-a-hotel in a Gilded-Age courtyard mansion, the exclusive Towers wing.

items.name: Crosby Street Hotel, Firmdale Hotels
items.description: Firmdale's English-country-house colour dropped into the heart of SoHo.

items.name: The Whitby Hotel, Firmdale Hotels
items.description: A joyful, art-filled Firmdale house a whisper from Fifth Avenue and Central Park.

items.name: The Lowell
items.description: A discreet townhouse hotel of wood fires and fresh flowers, old-money calm.

items.name: The Greenwich Hotel
items.description: Robert De Niro's Tribeca hideaway, a warm, worldly house with a lantern-lit pool.

items.name: The Fifth Avenue Hotel
items.description: A gilded mansion-and-tower debut, maximalist, romantic, the talk of NoMad.

items.name: Hotel Barrière Fouquet's New York
items.description: Parisian glamour on the Hudson side of Tribeca, the Champs-Élysées, restaged downtown.

items.name: Warren Street Hotel, Firmdale Hotels
items.description: Firmdale's downtown debut, the same fearless colour, now in Tribeca.

items.name: Trump International Hotel & Tower New York
items.description: Full Central Park frontage at Columbus Circle, big windows, big views.

items.name: Pendry Manhattan West
items.description: A sleek new-build in the Hudson Yards district, polished, contemporary, well-run.

items.name: Nine Orchard
items.description: A landmark 1912 bank turned design-led hotel, the coolest room downtown.

items.name: 1 Hotel Central Park
items.description: Nature-led calm steps from Central Park, reclaimed wood, living walls, easy comfort.

items.name: The Beekman, A Thompson Hotel
items.description: A breathtaking nine-storey Victorian atrium downtown, history with a modern pulse.

items.name: The Wall Street Hotel
items.description: A quietly elegant house in the old financial heart, a calm downtown residence.

items.name: The Mercer
items.description: The original SoHo loft hotel, spare, timeless, and endlessly cool.

items.name: The Bowery Hotel
items.description: A dimly-lit, velvet-and-candles downtown classic, romantic and a little bohemian.

items.name: The Ritz-Carlton New York, NoMad
items.description: A tall, contemporary Ritz-Carlton with a rooftop over the Empire State Building.

items.name: The Surrey, A Corinthia Hotel
items.description: A refined Upper East Side residence, newly reborn under Corinthia, quiet, gracious calm.

items.name: The Twenty Two New York
items.description: The London members'-club hotel's first New York address, buzzy and of-the-moment.

items.name: 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge
items.description: The best Manhattan-skyline view in the city, from the Brooklyn side of the river.

items.name: The New York EDITION
items.description: Understated elegance in a landmark clock tower over Madison Square Park.

items.name: The Ludlow Hotel
items.description: A relaxed, downtown-cool house on the Lower East Side, effortless and unpretentious.

items.name: Hotel Chelsea
items.description: The most legendary bohemian hotel in America, reborn, and steeped in its own myth.

items.name: Wythe Hotel
items.description: A converted Williamsburg factory with a rooftop bar and the skyline across the water.

items.name: Ace Hotel Brooklyn
items.description: A design-led, art-filled house in brownstone Brooklyn, relaxed and creative.

items.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
credentials: One of the world's great encyclopedic museums
Most-visited museum in the United States
items.description: Five thousand years of art in one building on Fifth Avenue, do the Temple of Dendur, the European paintings and the rooftop bar, then let the rest go; it's too big for one day.

items.name: The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA)
credentials: One of the world's foremost modern-art museums
items.description: Van Gogh's Starry Night, Monet's Water Lilies room, Warhol and Picasso, the modern canon in a light-filled building; go at opening or in the last two hours to dodge the crush.

items.name: The Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum
items.description: Frank Lloyd Wright's white spiral is the reason to come as much as the art, take the lift up and walk the ramp down past the Kandinskys.

items.name: The Frick Collection
items.description: A steel baron's Fifth Avenue mansion hung with Vermeer, Rembrandt and Bellini, reopened April 2025 after a $220m restoration that finally opened the family's upstairs rooms to the public; the most civilised hour of art in the city.

items.name: The Whitney Museum of American Art
items.description: Renzo Piano's museum of American art at the foot of the High Line, Hopper, O'Keeffe, Basquiat inside, and terraces that frame the Hudson and downtown skyline for free.

items.name: The Met Cloisters
items.description: The Met's medieval outpost, built from real French monastery cloisters on a bluff over the Hudson, the Unicorn Tapestries, herb gardens and river views make the subway ride uptown worth it. A quiet gem most visitors miss.

items.name: The Morgan Library & Museum
items.description: J.P. Morgan's private study and jewel-box library, Gutenberg Bibles, illuminated manuscripts and a domed rotunda in the financier's own home. Small, sumptuous, rarely crowded.

items.name: The American Museum of Natural History
items.description: Blue whale, dinosaur halls and the Rose planetarium plus the new Gilder science wing, the single best half-day in the city for children and multi-generational groups.

items.name: The Neue Galerie
items.description: A small mansion museum for German and Austrian art, home to Klimt's gold Woman in Gold, with Café Sabarsky downstairs for Viennese pastry. A refined pairing of art and Kaffeehaus.

items.name: The Noguchi Museum
items.description: Isamu Noguchi's own studio turned into a museum of stone sculpture around a still garden, a meditative escape a short hop across the river. Pair it with nearby Socrates Sculpture Park.

items.name: 9/11 Memorial & Museum
items.description: Two black reflecting pools in the tower footprints and a museum beneath ground zero, sobering and beautifully done; book the museum ahead and allow a quiet couple of hours.

items.name: Statue of Liberty & Ellis Island
items.description: The harbour crossing and the immigration halls are the real experience, book crown or pedestal access weeks ahead through your advisor, as they sell out; families can trace ancestors in the Ellis Island records.

items.name: Empire State Building
items.description: The 86th-floor open-air deck still delivers the classic New York view; the redone second-floor museum is genuinely good. Go at dusk to catch daylight and the lit city in one visit.

items.name: Top of the Rock, Rockefeller Center
items.description: The best skyline view precisely because it looks back at the Empire State and up Central Park, three open decks, no glass in your photos. The new 'Beam' rooftop experience is a fun add-on.

items.name: Summit One Vanderbilt
items.area: Midtown East / next to Grand Central
items.description: The most theatrical observation deck, mirrored rooms, glass-floor ledges over Madison Avenue and glass 'Ascent' lifts on the building's flank; part art installation, part view. Book a timed slot.

items.name: Edge at Hudson Yards
items.description: The Western Hemisphere's highest outdoor sky deck, with an angled glass floor and a lean-out corner over the West Side; adrenaline-seekers can add the 'City Climb' harnessed ascent up the building's exterior.

items.name: One World Observatory
items.description: Top of the tallest tower in the Western Hemisphere, a fast lift with a time-lapse of the city's rise, then harbour-to-Manhattan views. Best paired with the 9/11 Memorial below.

items.name: The Staten Island Ferry
items.description: The best free thing in New York, a 25-minute ride past the Statue of Liberty and the downtown skyline, no ticket, no queue. Ride out, turn around, ride back; go at golden hour.

items.name: Central Park
items.description: The 843-acre green heart of the city, the Bethesda Terrace, the Ramble, the Bow Bridge and the Reservoir loop; hire bikes or a rowboat, or take the kids to the zoo. A different world every season.

items.name: The High Line
items.description: A disused elevated freight line turned wild-planted walkway above the West Side, threading past galleries and river views; walk it end to end and step off into Chelsea's art scene or Hudson Yards.

items.name: Little Island
items.description: A pocket park floating over the Hudson on concrete 'tulips' by Heatherwick, undulating lawns, hidden overlooks and a small amphitheatre with summer performances. Free, and a lovely 20 minutes off the High Line.

items.name: Brooklyn Bridge
items.description: Walk the elevated wooden promenade from Manhattan into Brooklyn for the definitive skyline view; go early morning to have the cathedral-like stone arches nearly to yourself, then descend into DUMBO.

items.name: Brooklyn Bridge Park & DUMBO
items.description: Cobbled streets under the bridge, the Instagram-famous Washington Street view of the Manhattan Bridge, Jane's Carousel and a green waterfront that faces the whole downtown skyline. End the bridge walk here.

items.name: Washington Square Park & Greenwich Village
items.description: The marble arch, the fountain, the chess players and street musicians, the bohemian soul of the city, ringed by NYU and low townhouse streets perfect for aimless wandering.

items.name: The West Village
items.description: Crooked, tree-lined streets of red-brick townhouses, tiny bookshops and cafés, the prettiest walk in Manhattan and the loveliest for an unhurried morning. Bleecker and Perry streets are the postcard.

items.name: SoHo
credentials: SoHo-Cast Iron Historic District, National Historic Landmark
items.description: The world's densest run of cast-iron architecture, now a cobblestoned luxury shopping quarter, flagship boutiques below, ornate 19th-century facades above. Look up as much as into the windows.

items.name: Chinatown & Little Italy
items.description: One of the largest Chinese communities in the West, dim sum, tea shops and produce markets flowing into the last blocks of Little Italy on Mulberry Street; a sensory wander best done hungry.

items.name: The Lower East Side
items.description: The old immigrant tenement district turned gallery-and-cocktail neighbourhood; the Tenement Museum tells the story through restored apartments, then the streets deliver vintage shops and the New Museum.

items.name: Harlem
items.description: The capital of Black American culture, a Sunday gospel service, the Apollo Theater, soul food on Lenox Avenue and the Studio Museum; take a guided walk to read the history in the brownstones.

items.name: Williamsburg
items.description: Brooklyn's design-and-nightlife capital, independent boutiques, rooftop bars and the best Manhattan-skyline sunset in the city from the East River waterfront. Take the ferry over for the arrival.

items.name: The Apollo Theater
items.description: The stage where Ella Fitzgerald, James Brown and Aretha were made, catch the legendary Amateur Night or a show, or take the daytime tour of a true American music landmark.

items.name: Broadway & the Theater District
items.description: The world's benchmark for musical theatre, book a marquee show months ahead through your advisor; family groups can't go wrong with The Lion King or Aladdin. Skip Times Square itself once you've seen it.

items.name: Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts
items.description: The Metropolitan Opera, the New York Philharmonic and City Ballet around a floodlit travertine plaza and fountain, dress up for a Met Opera night, one of the great evenings out in the city.

items.name: Carnegie Hall
items.description: The most storied concert hall in America, with acoustics musicians travel the world to play, a recital here is a bucket-list evening; a backstage tour reveals the history if you can't catch a show.

items.name: Village Vanguard & the Village jazz clubs
items.description: The basement room where Coltrane and Bill Evans recorded live albums, still the holy ground of jazz. Book the early set; pair it with Blue Note or Smalls nearby for a proper night of music.

items.name: Grand Central Terminal
items.description: Not a station so much as a Beaux-Arts cathedral, the celestial-ceiling main concourse, the Whispering Gallery and an oyster bar in the vaults below. Free, always open, and quietly astonishing.

items.name: The New York Public Library (Stephen A. Schwarzman Building)
items.description: The marble-lion library whose Rose Reading Room, a football-field of chandeliers and painted clouds, is open to anyone who walks in; catch a free treasures exhibition and step next door into Bryant Park.

items.name: Rockefeller Center
items.description: An Art Deco city-within-a-city, the golden Prometheus and the sunken plaza (ice-skating in winter, the giant tree in December), Radio City next door and Top of the Rock above. The heart of Midtown.

items.name: St. Patrick's Cathedral
items.description: The great white Gothic-Revival cathedral facing Rockefeller Center, step in from the Fifth Avenue bustle for the soaring nave and rose window; a five-minute pause that resets the whole day.

items.name: The Oculus & World Trade Center
items.description: Calatrava's soaring white-ribbed transit hall, like a bird or a whale's skeleton in marble, now a luxury shopping concourse; the most dramatic piece of new architecture downtown, and free to walk through.

items.name: Chelsea gallery district
items.description: The world's densest concentration of contemporary art galleries, Gagosian, David Zwirner, Hauser & Wirth and dozens more, all free to enter. Spend a Saturday afternoon drifting between shows off the High Line.

items.name: Chelsea Market
items.description: A former Nabisco biscuit factory turned covered food hall, lobster, tacos, artisan pastry and design shops in brick-and-pipe arcades; graze your way through, then step straight onto the High Line above.

items.name: Grand Central Market & Great Northern Food Hall
items.description: Within and beside the terminal, a European-style market of cheese, seafood and fresh bread, and Nordic food stalls under the arches. A civilised graze while you admire the building.

items.name: Smorgasburg
items.description: America's largest open-air food market, a hundred-odd vendors of everything from ramen burgers to mango sticky rice, with the Manhattan skyline behind. Weekends only, and a great way to eat your way through Brooklyn.

items.name: Fifth Avenue & Madison Avenue shopping
items.description: The full spectrum of luxury, the marquee flagships and Bergdorf Goodman on Fifth, the quieter European maisons and galleries up Madison. Your advisor can arrange private appointments and after-hours access.

items.name: SoHo boutiques
items.description: The most stylish shopping in the city, flagship fashion, concept stores and independent design along cast-iron blocks; less crowded and more curated than Fifth Avenue, and made for wandering on foot.

items.name: A Central Park bike or pedicab ride
items.description: The loveliest way to see the whole park in an hour, hire bikes at Columbus Circle, or take a guided pedicab to the film locations and hidden corners. Gentler and more private than the carriage horses.

items.name: A Hudson River sunset sail
items.description: Board a classic schooner or private yacht for a sail past the Statue of Liberty as the skyline lights up, the single most romantic hour in New York, and easily chartered privately through your advisor.

items.name: A Manhattan helicopter tour
items.description: Fifteen minutes over the harbour, the Statue of Liberty and the length of the skyline, the view that puts the whole city in one frame; ask your advisor about doors-off or private charters.

items.name: The Roosevelt Island Tramway
items.description: A commuter aerial cable-car, on a subway swipe, that glides over the East River beside the Queensboro Bridge for a five-minute skyline ride; a quiet thrill most visitors never find.

items.name: Prospect Park & the Brooklyn Botanic Garden
items.description: The same designers' 'better' park than Central Park, meadows, a lake and a ravine with fewer crowds, beside a botanic garden famed for its spring cherry blossom and Japanese pond. A perfect Brooklyn morning.

items.name: Green-Wood Cemetery
items.description: A 478-acre Victorian garden cemetery of rolling hills, glacial ponds and Gothic gates, resting place of Basquiat and Bernstein, with the best hidden harbour view in Brooklyn. Wildly atmospheric and almost empty.

items.name: The Cathedral of St. John the Divine
items.description: The largest Gothic cathedral in the world, still famously unfinished, a vast, cool, half-built nave with a peacock in the close. Deeply atmospheric, and paired well with a Columbia University stroll.

items.name: The Tenement Museum
items.description: Restored immigrant apartments in a preserved 1863 tenement, told through the real families who lived there, the most moving history lesson in the city, and resonant for anyone whose own family emigrated. Book a tour ahead.

items.name: Storm King Art Center
items.description: A 500-acre open-air sculpture park where monumental Calders, Serras and Goldsworthys sit in rolling meadows and woods, a full day of art and landscape; hire bikes on arrival. A superb warm-weather day trip.

items.name: Dia Beacon
items.description: A former Nabisco box factory turned vast, daylit museum of minimalist and land art, Richter, Serra, Judd on a monumental scale. Reachable by a scenic Metro-North ride along the Hudson; the most serene art day out.

items.name: The Hamptons
items.description: The summer-weekend playground of Manhattan's elite, ocean beaches, hedge-lined estates, farm stands and East Hampton village; best mid-week to avoid the crowds. Your advisor can arrange a house or a beach club.

items.name: Eleven Madison Park
items.description: Daniel Humm's plant-based three-star, the most talked-about fine-dining room in America.

items.name: Le Bernardin
items.description: Eric Ripert's temple to seafood, three stars held for decades, and never a slip.

items.name: Per Se
items.description: Thomas Keller's New York flagship, a hushed room over Central Park, at the summit.

items.name: Jungsik
items.description: Yim Jungsik's modern Korean, the cuisine reimagined at the very highest level.

items.name: Sushi Sho
items.description: The city's newest three-star, a revered Tokyo master's edomae omakase.

items.name: Atomix
items.description: The Parks' Korean tasting counter, named the best restaurant in North America.

items.name: Masa
items.description: Masa Takayama's austere, extravagant sushi, still among the costliest meals in America.

items.name: Daniel
items.description: Daniel Boulud's grand French dining room, the Upper East Side's most elegant table.

items.name: Jean-Georges
items.description: Jean-Georges Vongerichten's flagship, light, precise French with a park view.

items.name: The Modern
items.description: Refined American cooking overlooking MoMA's sculpture garden, art on both sides of the glass.

items.name: Gabriel Kreuther
items.description: Alsatian-French cooking of real soul, overlooking Bryant Park.

items.name: Aska
items.description: Fredrik Berselius's Nordic tasting menu in a candlelit Williamsburg townhouse.

items.name: Atera
items.description: An intimate Tribeca counter of exacting, seasonal tasting menus.

items.name: Saga
items.description: A tasting menu high in a landmark 1930s skyscraper, the view is part of the meal.

items.name: César
items.description: A French-Japanese two-star that arrived fully formed, precise and personal.

items.name: Chef's Table at Brooklyn Fare
items.description: An intense, seafood-led counter, one of the city's most serious tasting experiences.

items.name: Joo Ok
items.description: A refined Korean tasting menu, newly elevated to two stars, quiet, considered, exact.

items.name: Sushi Noz
items.description: A hinoki-wood counter of pure edomae craft, sushi as meditation.

items.name: Odo
items.description: A serene kaiseki counter hidden behind a tea room, Japan, faithfully rendered.

items.name: Huso
items.description: A caviar-and-seafood tasting counter of great luxury, newly starred.

items.name: Aquavit
items.description: The city's benchmark for Nordic cooking, cool, clean, and quietly luxurious.

items.name: Semma
items.description: The only Indian restaurant in America to hold a Michelin star, South India, uncompromised.

items.name: Café Carmellini
items.description: Andrew Carmellini's grand, romantic Italian-French room inside The Fifth Avenue Hotel.

items.name: Torrisi
items.description: Italian-American cooking with a New-York swagger, in the landmark Puck Building.

items.name: Rezdôra
items.description: A love letter to Emilia-Romagna, the city's most wanted pasta.

items.name: Le Coucou
items.description: A beautiful, candlelit ode to classical French cooking in the heart of SoHo.

items.name: Crown Shy
items.description: James Kent's downtown room, inventive, generous, and consistently excellent.

items.name: The Dining Room at Gramercy Tavern
items.description: A New York institution, seasonal American cooking of unwavering grace.

items.name: COTE
items.description: A Korean steakhouse of real refinement, the butcher's counter meets the tasting menu.

items.name: Le Pavillon
items.description: Daniel Boulud's soaring, garden-like room of vegetable- and seafood-led French cooking.

items.name: Café Boulud at Maison Barnes
items.description: Daniel Boulud's warm, seasonal café, refined French with an easy grace.

items.name: Sushi Nakazawa
items.description: A joyful, generous omakase from a Jiro-trained master, sushi with a smile.

items.name: Corima
items.description: Modern Northern Mexican cooking that earned a star within a year of opening.

items.name: Dirt Candy
items.description: Amanda Cohen's pioneering vegetable tasting menu, the case for vegetables, made joyfully.

items.name: The Four Horsemen
items.description: A wine bar that quietly became one of the country's best restaurants.

items.name: Bridges
items.description: A newly-starred Chinatown room bringing quiet French finesse to a downtown corner.

items.name: Yamada
items.description: A precise new Japanese counter that earned its star straight out of the gate.

items.name: Frevo
items.description: An intimate tasting menu hidden behind an art-gallery door, French with a Brazilian pulse.

items.name: Kono
items.description: A tiny yakitori counter of great purity, every part of the bird over charcoal.

items.name: Le Veau d'Or
items.description: New York's oldest French bistro, lovingly revived, a piece of the city's soul.

items.name: Oxomoco
items.description: Wood-fired, one-star Mexican cooking in a sunlit Greenpoint room.

items.name: Via Carota
items.description: The West Village trattoria everyone wants a table at, simple, perfect, always full.

items.name: Dhamaka
items.description: Unapologetic, rustic Indian cooking that pulls no punches, a love letter to the regions.

items.name: Bungalow
items.description: Vikas Khanna's ode to Indian country-club dining, glamorous, generous, joyful.

items.name: Cardamom
items.description: Modern Indian cooking with a light, contemporary hand, Bib-listed and easy to love.

items.name: Chutney Masala
items.description: Warm, well-made Indian cooking that quietly earned the inspectors' nod.

items.name: HanGawi
items.description: A serene, shoes-off Korean temple restaurant, entirely vegetarian, and quietly special.

items.name: Coqodaq
items.description: A glamorous Korean fried-chicken-and-Champagne room, serious fun, seriously good.

items.name: Bonnie's
items.description: Cantonese-American cooking with a Brooklyn wit, nostalgic and inventive at once.

items.name: Atla
items.description: Bright, all-day Mexican cooking from the Cosme team, fresh, light, and always buzzing.

items.name: Dim Sum Go Go
items.description: A Chinatown stalwart doing precise, handmade dim sum, credentialed and beloved.

items.name: CheLi
items.description: Shanghainese home cooking done with real care, a Bib-listed crowd favourite.

items.name: Bemelmans Bar
credentials: A globally historic cocktail bar, inside The Carlyle
items.description: The most beautiful bar in New York, Ludwig Bemelmans' murals, a grand piano, a perfect martini.

items.name: The King Cole Bar
credentials: A globally historic cocktail bar, inside The St. Regis
items.description: The birthplace of the Bloody Mary, beneath Maxfield Parrish's mural, old-money New York.

items.name: The Dead Rabbit
items.description: A former World's Best Bar reviving the lost art of the New York-Irish tavern.

items.name: Katana Kitten
credentials: Former World's Best Bar in America
items.description: A Japanese-American izakaya bar that has ranked among the world's best for years.

items.name: Double Chicken Please
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars, former No. 1 in North America
items.description: An inventive back-room bar that was recently ranked the best in North America.

items.name: Attaboy
items.description: A no-menu speakeasy where you name a spirit and a mood, bespoke drinks, no fuss.

items.name: The Aviary NYC
credentials: A bar of international standing, from the Alinea Group
items.description: A theatrical cocktail laboratory high in the Mandarin Oriental, drinks as edible art.

items.name: Overstory
items.description: Cocktails on the 64th floor with a 360-degree sweep of the harbour and the skyline.

items.name: The Rooftop at Pier 17
credentials: A landmark rooftop venue at the Seaport
items.description: Drinks and skyline views by the Brooklyn Bridge, the river breeze on a summer night.

items.name: Employees Only
items.description: A speakeasy that helped start the modern cocktail revival, buzzy well past midnight.

plan.heading: 4 days in New York, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle into The Mark on the Upper East Side, then coffee and the morning light in Central Park.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Whitney and a slow walk of the High Line down to the Meatpacking District.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Le Bernardin, the tasting menu, a table booked well ahead.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Met at opening with a private guide, an hour or two, not the whole thing.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at The Modern, then the galleries at MoMA at your own pace.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Cocktails at The Aviary and dinner at Eleven Madison Park.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The 9/11 Memorial early, then the ferry past the harbour with the skyline behind.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: SoHo and Tribeca for the galleries and the makers, lunch at Frenchette.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A jazz set at the Village Vanguard, late supper at Balthazar.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Breakfast at the hotel, then the Frick Collection in its restored halls.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A last walk through the Park and Madison Avenue before the afternoon flight.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: An early table at Daniel if the schedule allows, then the airport.

items.name: Tribeca / SoHo
items.description: Cast-iron loft streets, galleries and the best downtown dining; suits design lovers and repeat visitors.

items.name: West Village
items.description: Leafy, low-rise and romantic, with the city's most walkable streets; suits couples and anyone wanting charm over spectacle.

items.name: Upper East Side
items.description: Museum Mile, Central Park and the grand old hotels; suits families and first-timers who want the classic uptown address.

events.name: Tribeca Festival
events.note: Robert De Niro's downtown film festival, when premieres and talks take over lower Manhattan for a fortnight.

events.name: US Open (tennis)
events.note: The season's final Grand Slam in Flushing Meadows, the loudest and latest-running of the four.

events.name: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade
events.note: The giant-balloon parade down Central Park West on Thanksgiving morning, the start of the city's holiday season.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay in the low 60s off Central Park or in the West Village for quiet luxury; the ESTA must be secured before an Indian passport holder travels, and dinner at the best tables (or a Broadway premiere) needs booking weeks ahead.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Arrive at JFK or Newark (EWR); a pre-booked black car or a member service like Blade's helicopter transfer from JFK avoids the bridge-and-tunnel crawl into Manhattan.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Manhattan is best walked, with a private car or well-vetted black-car app for cross-town and downtown moves; skip driving yourself.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: US eSIM (AT&T/Verizon/T-Mobile) or an international eSIM works everywhere; coverage and hotel Wi-Fi are excellent, subway signal now included.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: US dollar; cards and Apple Pay are universal and cash is rarely needed; tip roughly 20% at restaurants and $2–5 per bag or service.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Late April-June and September-October are the kind windows, mild and clear; avoid the humid heat of July-August and the deep cold and slush of January-February.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Air India flies Delhi-New York (JFK and Newark) nonstop in about 15-16 hours, with United and American also nonstop from Delhi; from Mumbai and Bengaluru it is typically one stop via a Gulf or European hub in J or F. If connecting, Emirates via Dubai offers the strongest first-class and lounge experience.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required beyond routine; the ESTA or B-1/B-2 visa must be arranged in advance for the Indian passport. Manhattan is safe with ordinary big-city awareness. Tap water is excellent.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian is effortless and Jain is achievable in the Indian restaurants; the city has serious Indian dining. Consider Dhamaka or Semma (Michelin-starred South Indian) for something beyond the ordinary.
